name: Paris
subtitle: Lutetia to the Revolution
description: Paris from Roman Lutetia on the left bank to the eve of the Revolution: the Seine and its islands, the Cité, the right-bank Ville and the left-bank University, inside the walls of Philippe Auguste and Charles V. Positions are projected from real coordinates; the drawing is an illustration, not a survey.

water.name: Bras de Grammont
water.blurb: The narrow arm between the right bank and the Île Louviers, a timber yard for most of its history; it was filled in in 1843 and is now the boulevard Morland.

water.name: Seine (petit bras)
water.blurb: The south arm of the Seine, narrow and shallow, between the Cité and the left bank. The Petit Pont has crossed it since Roman times, always on the line of the rue Saint-Jacques.

water.name: Seine
water.blurb: Sequana to the Romans. The river made Paris: the merchants of the water (the nautae, later the marchands de l'eau) ran its trade, and the city's arms are still a ship. Wine, wood, grain and hay came down it to the right-bank ports of the Grève and the École.

water.name: Bièvre
water.blurb: A little river from the south, lined from the 15th century with tanners, dyers and the Gobelins tapestry works, and thick with their waste. The monks of Saint-Victor diverted part of it through their abbey in the 12th century.

hills.name: Montagne Sainte-Geneviève
hills.blurb: The limestone hill of the left bank, Mons Lucotitius to the Romans, who built their forum on its shoulder. Saint Geneviève was buried on the summit about 502; the abbey named after her, then the colleges of the University, covered it.

hills.name: Butte Saint-Roch
hills.blurb: A mound of rubbish and spoil outside the Saint-Honoré gate, crowned with windmills; Joan of Arc was wounded attacking the city near here in 1429. It was levelled from the 1660s for the new quarter round the rue de Richelieu.

hills.name: Monceau Saint-Gervais
hills.blurb: A low gravel rise on the right bank, safe from the floods, where the first settlement north of the river grew round the church of Saint-Gervais.

roads.name: Cardo maximus (rue Saint-Jacques)
roads.blurb: The main north–south street of Lutetia, paved and colonnaded, crossing the island and climbing the hill toward Orléans. The rue Saint-Jacques still follows it.

roads.name: Western cardo (boulevard Saint-Michel line)
roads.blurb: A parallel street to the west, past the Cluny baths; the line of the medieval rue de la Harpe and today's boulevard Saint-Michel.

roads.name: Decumanus (rue des Écoles line)
roads.blurb: An east–west street of the Roman grid; its exact line is reconstructed from scattered finds.

roads.name: Road to Italy (rue Mouffetard)
roads.blurb: The Roman road south-east toward Lyon and Italy, up the Montagne and down the far side; the rue de la Montagne-Sainte-Geneviève, rue Descartes and rue Mouffetard follow it.

roads.name: Road to Senlis (rue Saint-Martin)
roads.blurb: The Roman road north from the Grand Pont, along a gravel ridge above the marsh; the rue Saint-Martin follows it.

roads.name: Road to Melun (rue Saint-Antoine)
roads.blurb: The road east along the right bank toward Melun and Sens; later the rue Saint-Antoine.

roads.name: Rue de la Juiverie (the island's high street)
roads.blurb: The street across the Cité from the Petit Pont to the bridge over the north arm, on the line of the Roman cardo: the rue du Marché-Palu, the rue de la Juiverie (the Jews' street until their expulsion in 1182) and the rue de la Lanterne.

roads.name: Rue Saint-Jacques
roads.blurb: The Roman cardo, and the pilgrims' road to Compostela: the great street of the University, of the Dominicans (the 'Jacobins'), and from the 1470s of the printers and booksellers.

roads.name: Rue Saint-Martin
roads.blurb: The old Roman road north, past Saint-Merry and the priory of Saint-Martin-des-Champs toward Senlis and Flanders.

roads.name: Rue Saint-Denis
roads.blurb: The Grande Rue: the royal way from the Châtelet to the abbey of Saint-Denis, taken by kings entering Paris and by their funerals leaving it.

roads.name: Rue Saint-Honoré
roads.blurb: The road west from the Halles toward Normandy, past Saint-Honoré's church and, outside the gate, the hospital of the Quinze-Vingts. By the 18th century the richest shopping street in Paris.

roads.name: Rue Saint-Antoine
roads.blurb: The widest street of medieval Paris, used for tournaments and royal entries; Henri II was mortally wounded jousting here in 1559. It runs out past the Bastille to the abbey of Saint-Antoine.

roads.name: Rue du Temple
roads.blurb: The street from the Grève to the Templars' enclosure, through the Marais.

roads.name: Rue Montmartre
roads.blurb: The road north from Saint-Eustache toward the hill and abbey of Montmartre.

roads.name: Rue de la Verrerie
roads.blurb: The glassmakers' street, the old east–west route behind the Grève through the parish of Saint-Merry.

roads.name: Rue Galande and rue Saint-Victor
roads.blurb: From the Petit Pont past the place Maubert, where the poorest scholars heard their lectures, to the abbey of Saint-Victor.

roads.name: Rue de la Harpe
roads.blurb: The University's western street, from the Pont Saint-Michel past the Cluny ruins to the Porte Saint-Michel.

roads.name: Rue Saint-André-des-Arts and rue de Buci
roads.blurb: The road from the Cité bridges west to the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and its fair.

roads.name: Rue de Vaugirard
roads.blurb: The longest street of Paris, toward the village of Vaugirard, past the Luxembourg palace (1615).

roads.name: Rue Dauphine
roads.blurb: Cut in 1607 through the gardens of the Grands-Augustins to carry the traffic of the new Pont Neuf to the faubourg Saint-Germain.

roads.name: Rue de Richelieu
roads.blurb: The street laid out over the levelled Butte Saint-Roch beside Richelieu's palace (the Palais-Royal), home of the royal library.

roads.name: Rue de Grenelle and rue du Bac
roads.blurb: The ferry road from the Pont Royal into the faubourg Saint-Germain, the quarter of aristocratic hôtels between court and garden.

roads.name: The Boulevards (Nouveau Cours)
roads.blurb: Louis XIV had the right-bank wall levelled from 1670 and planted with four rows of elms: a promenade for coaches, then the theatres, cafés and puppet shows of the boulevard du Temple.

roads.name: Champs-Élysées
roads.blurb: Le Nôtre's avenue (1667) continuing the Tuileries axis west across the Place Louis XV into the country.

walls.name: Late Roman wall of the Cité
walls.blurb: Built about 300 CE of reused stone from the forum and the arena, it shrank Lutetia to the island. Repaired, it held the Vikings off in 885–86 and still girdled the Cité around 1000.

walls.name: Wall of Philippe Auguste (right bank)
walls.blurb: Built 1190–1209 on the king's order before he left on crusade, paid for by the burghers: about 2.5 km on this bank, 2.5 to 3 m thick and 6 to 8 m high, a round tower every 70 m or so, gates on every road out.

walls.name: Wall of Philippe Auguste (left bank)
walls.blurb: The left-bank half, built about 1200–1215 by the king himself, from the Tour de Nesle over the shoulder of the Montagne to the Tournelle. It enclosed the University and still stood, ditched anew, in the 16th century.

walls.name: Wall of Charles V
walls.blurb: Begun in 1356 by the provost Étienne Marcel and finished under Charles V about 1383: an earth rampart faced with stone behind a double ditch, enclosing the new right-bank suburbs and the Louvre, with the Bastille guarding the east.

bridges.name: Petit Pont
bridges.blurb: The short bridge over the south arm, on the line of the cardo. Swept away by floods again and again and rebuilt in timber or stone; in 885 its tower was the last post to fall to the Vikings.

bridges.name: Petit Pont
bridges.blurb: Rebuilt in stone by Bishop Maurice de Sully in 1185 and many times after, lined with houses, guarded at its left-bank end by the Petit Châtelet, the provost's prison.

bridges.name: Grand Pont
bridges.blurb: The Roman bridge over the north arm, on the line of the cardo where the Pont Notre-Dame now stands.

bridges.name: Grand Pont
bridges.blurb: Rebuilt in the 9th century a little downstream, on the line of the later Pont au Change, with water mills beneath it and a tower at its right-bank head (the future Grand Châtelet).

bridges.name: Pont au Change
bridges.blurb: The bridge of the money-changers and goldsmiths.

bridges.name: Pont Notre-Dame
bridges.blurb: The bridge of houses, rebuilt in stone 1500–1512.

bridges.name: Pont Saint-Michel
bridges.blurb: First built 1378–87, lined with houses, carried away by ice and floods several times and rebuilt in stone in 1616–24, still with houses on it in 1789.

bridges.name: Pont Marie
bridges.blurb: Built 1614–35 by the developer Christophe Marie to open the new Île Saint-Louis; houses lined it until 1788.

bridges.name: Pont de la Tournelle
bridges.blurb: Stone bridge of 1656 from the Île Saint-Louis to the quai de la Tournelle.

bridges.name: Pont Rouge
bridges.blurb: A wooden footbridge, painted red, between the Cité and the Île Saint-Louis.

bridges.name: Pont au Double
bridges.blurb: Built 1634 for the Hôtel-Dieu; the toll was a double denier.

bridges.name: Pont Royal
bridges.blurb: Louis XIV's stone bridge of 1685–89 from the Tuileries to the faubourg Saint-Germain, replacing a wooden one.

blocks.name: La Ville inside the wall of Charles V
Saint-Roch, the Place Vendôme and the Carrousel
Palais-Royal and the rue de Richelieu
Saint-Bernard and the Halle aux Vins

gardens.name: Gardens of the Hôtel des Tournelles

districts.name: La Cité
districts.description: The island of king and bishop: the royal palace at the west end, Notre-Dame and the Hôtel-Dieu at the east, and between them a maze of lanes and some twenty parish churches.

districts.name: La Ville
districts.description: The right bank of the merchants: the ports of the Grève, the Halles, the butchers, the changers and the Hôtel de Ville of the provost of the merchants.

districts.name: L'Université
districts.description: The left bank of masters and students, who spoke Latin, hence the Latin Quarter: colleges, convents of the friars, booksellers and parchment-makers inside the wall.

districts.name: Faubourg Saint-Germain
districts.description: The aristocracy's quarter since Louis XIV: grand hôtels between court and garden on the rue de Grenelle, rue de Varenne and rue de l'Université.

districts.name: Faubourg Saint-Antoine
districts.description: The furniture-makers' faubourg outside the Bastille, free of guild rules under the abbey's protection; its workmen marched on the fortress in July 1789.

periods.label: Roman Lutetia
periods.summary: Lutetia of the Parisii: a modest Gallo-Roman town laid out on a grid on the left-bank slope of Mons Lucotitius, with a forum astride the cardo, three public baths fed by an aqueduct from Wissous, an arena, and a quarter of temples and houses on the island. Limestone quarried on the spot, timber and tile; a wooden bridge at each end of the island.
periods.feel: Boatmen calling on the river, smoke from the baths' furnaces, the clink of stonecutters working the local limestone.

houses.title: Houses of Lutetia
houses.text: Rectangular houses of rubble and timber framing on stone footings, plastered and roofed with red tile, set along the gridded streets of the left bank; shops open onto the street, small gardens and wells behind.

outskirts.title: Vineyards and villas
outskirts.text: Vines and gardens on the slopes of the hill, a few villas, potters' kilns and the cemeteries lining the roads south toward Orléans and Italy.

periods.label: Capetian Paris
periods.summary: Clovis made Paris his seat about 508; the Vikings besieged the Cité in 885–86. Around 1000, under Robert the Pious, the town is still mostly the island inside its Roman wall, with the palace at one end and the cathedral of Saint-Étienne at the other. Walled abbeys stand in the fields; small bourgs grow round the right-bank port and the churches of the left bank.
periods.population: perhaps 20,000 around 1000, growing fast in the 12th century
periods.feel: Monastery bells across the meadows, the creak of mill wheels under the Grand Pont, mud and woodsmoke in the island's lanes.

houses.title: Houses of the Cité
houses.text: Narrow timber-framed houses with wattle-and-daub infill on stone cellars, two or three storeys, thatched or shingled, packed along the lanes of the island and the little bourgs at the bridgeheads.

outskirts.title: Bourgs, vineyards and marsh
outskirts.text: Clusters of houses round the abbeys and parish churches, enclosed vineyards (clos) on the left-bank hill, and the drained marsh gardens of the right bank.

periods.label: Gothic Paris
periods.summary: The largest city in Christian Europe, inside the new wall of Philippe Auguste (1190–1215). Saint Louis reigns; Notre-Dame is nearly finished and the Sainte-Chapelle has just been consecrated (1248). Three towns in one: the Cité of king and bishop, the merchants' Ville on the right bank with the Halles and the Grève, and the University's Latin Quarter on the left.
periods.feel: Students arguing in Latin, criers calling wine and baths through the streets, cart wheels on the new paving, the reek of the Grande Boucherie.

houses.title: Gabled houses of the Ville
houses.text: Tall, narrow timber-framed houses, gable end to the street, on stone ground floors with shop counters folding down onto the street; plastered fronts, jettied upper storeys, tile or slate roofs. Courtyards, wells and privies behind.

outskirts.title: Faubourgs and clos
outskirts.text: Outside the wall: abbey bourgs, vineyards and walled clos, market gardens in the drained Marais, windmills, and hamlets strung along the roads.

periods.label: Renaissance Paris
periods.summary: The capital of Henri II, now behind the right-bank wall of Charles V with the Bastille at its east gate. Pierre Lescot is rebuilding the Louvre in the new Italian manner, the Hôtel de Ville is rising on the Grève, and the Pont Notre-Dame carries a street of uniform houses. Printers fill the rue Saint-Jacques; religious war is coming.
periods.feel: Presses thumping in the rue Saint-Jacques, hawkers' cries, church bells by the hundred, the stink of the tanneries and the river.

houses.title: Houses of Renaissance Paris
houses.text: Gabled timber-framed houses of four and five storeys, many now plastered over against fire, on stone ground floors with shops; noble hôtels of stone between court and garden appear in the Marais and the faubourg Saint-Germain.

outskirts.title: Faubourgs
outskirts.text: Suburbs spilling past the gates: the fair-town of Saint-Germain, tanners and dyers on the Bièvre, market gardens of the Marais, windmills on the mounds.

periods.label: Paris on the Eve of the Revolution
periods.summary: The walls are gone, turned into tree-lined boulevards; the Farmers-General customs wall (1785–90) lies far out of frame. Place Louis XV opens west of the Tuileries gardens, the new church of Sainte-Geneviève (the Panthéon) is nearly done, the Pont Neuf is the city's street. On 14 July 1789 the crowd takes the Bastille.
periods.feel: Coaches rattling on paving stones, newsboys crying pamphlets, café talk at the Palais-Royal, mud and horse dung everywhere.

houses.title: Houses of 18th-century Paris
houses.text: Five- and six-storey houses of pale limestone or plaster over timber, regular windows, mansard roofs with dormers; shops on the ground floor, the bourgeois on the first floor, the poor in the garrets. Building height is capped by royal regulation.

outskirts.title: Faubourgs and gardens
outskirts.text: Aristocratic hôtels with long gardens in the faubourg Saint-Germain, artisans' courts in the faubourg Saint-Antoine, convent gardens and market plots toward the customs wall.

landmarks.name: Notre-Dame de Paris

lutetia-200.note: A temple, probably of Jupiter, stood at the island's east end: the Pillar of the Boatmen, dedicated under Tiberius, was dug up beneath the choir in 1711.

capetian-1000.name: Cathedral of Saint-Étienne
capetian-1000.note: The old cathedral of Saint-Étienne, a five-aisled basilica probably of the 6th century, stood a little west, under the later parvis. Bishop Maurice de Sully pulled it down to begin Notre-Dame in 1163.

philippe-1250.note: Nearly finished: choir 1163–82, nave about 1200, west front and towers by about 1250. Chapels are going in between the buttresses and the transept fronts with their great roses are about to be rebuilt.

valois-1550.note: Complete since about 1345, with the spire over the crossing, the jubé screen and the choir enclosure; the parvis is crowded with houses and the bishop's palace lies along the south flank.

louis-1789.note: Modernised by the canons: medieval glass replaced with clear panes, the jubé gone, Soufflot's cut through the central portal (1771). The decayed spire was taken down from 1786.

landmarks.summary: The cathedral of Paris, begun in 1163 at the east end of the Cité: twin square towers, three portals and a rose window on the west front, flying buttresses round a five-aisled nave.
details: Bishop Maurice de Sully began it in 1163 on the site of the old cathedral of Saint-Étienne. The choir was vaulted by 1182, the nave by about 1200 and the west front with its 69 m towers by about 1250. Flying buttresses, used here early, carry the high vaults; the transept roses (about 1250–60) are among the largest of the century.

The miniature shows the cathedral as finished in the 14th century: the west front with its gallery of kings and rose, the double aisles and chapels, the double-flight buttresses round the apse and the 13th-century spire over the crossing. Sculpture, gargoyles and the bishop's palace are left out.
landmarks.function: Cathedral of the bishops of Paris

landmarks.name: Sainte-Chapelle

capetian-1000.note: The palace chapel of Saint-Nicolas stood in the royal enclosure here.

philippe-1250.note: Brand new: consecrated on 26 April 1248 to house the Crown of Thorns, bought by Louis IX from the Latin emperor of Constantinople for more than the chapel itself cost.

valois-1550.note: The spire is Charles VII's of the 1450s–60s. The relics are shown to the crowd from a balcony each Good Friday; the lower chapel serves the palace staff.

louis-1789.note: The spire burned in 1630 and was rebuilt. The chapel still serves the law courts that now fill the palace; in 1791 the relics will be removed and the spire pulled down.

landmarks.summary: Louis IX's palace chapel, built 1242–48 as a giant reliquary for the Crown of Thorns: an upper chapel that is almost all glass, under a steep roof and a slender spire.
details: Two chapels one above the other: a low lower chapel for the household, and the upper chapel for the king, 20 m high and walled with fifteen windows of stained glass between thin buttresses. Its 1,113 glass panels tell the Bible from Genesis to the arrival of the relics in Paris. The west front has a rose (rebuilt about 1490).

The miniature shows the tall narrow body with its gabled windows, the corner turrets of the west front, the porch, the apse of seven bays and the lead-covered spire about 75 m above the ground. The spire has been rebuilt several times; this follows the usual reconstruction.

landmarks.name: Palais de la Cité

lutetia-200.note: The west end of the island probably held a late Roman fortified residence, where the governor and, in 358–360, the Caesar Julian lived; its remains are fragmentary.

capetian-1000.note: Robert the Pious's palace: a square stone keep, a great hall and a chapel inside a wall at the island's west end, with the royal garden on the point.

philippe-1250.note: Saint Louis's palace: Louis VI's keep, the old great hall, the new Tour Bonbec on the quay and, in the court, the Sainte-Chapelle.

valois-1550.note: Philip the Fair's rebuilding (1298–1315): the twin-naved Grand-Salle, the Tours César and d'Argent on the quay, Charles V's clock tower (1371). The kings have left; the Parlement sits here.

louis-1789.name: Palais de Justice
louis-1789.note: Burned in 1618 and 1776 and rebuilt for the law courts; the old keep was demolished in 1778. The Conciergerie towers hold the prison.

landmarks.summary: The palace of the kings of France on the west end of the Cité, then the seat of the Parlement and the law courts; its towers on the quay house the Conciergerie prison.
details: Merovingian and Capetian kings lived here; Philip the Fair rebuilt it from 1298 as the grandest palace in Europe, with a great hall of two vaulted naves lined with statues of the kings. After Étienne Marcel's men murdered two marshals before the dauphin in 1358, the kings moved to the Louvre and the Hôtel Saint-Pol, leaving the palace to the Parlement and the courts.

The miniature shows the north range on the quay: the three round towers of the Conciergerie with slate cones, the square clock tower at the east corner, the Grand-Salle behind and the old keep. The south courts and markets of the Galerie Mercière are simplified.
landmarks.function: Royal palace, then Parlement, law courts and prison

landmarks.name: The Louvre

capetian-1000.note: Fields and the river bank west of the bourg of Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois; the name may come from a wolf-hunting lodge (louverie), but no one knows.

philippe-1250.name: Louvre castle
philippe-1250.note: Philippe Auguste's fortress of about 1190–1202, just outside his new wall to guard the river downstream: a square curtain with ten towers round the 30 m Grosse Tour, which holds the royal treasury and archives.

valois-1550.note: Charles V made the castle a palace; Francis I razed the Grosse Tour in 1528, and since 1546 Pierre Lescot has been replacing the west wing with a Renaissance wing carved by Jean Goujon.

louis-1789.note: Lescot's wing has grown into the Cour Carrée, closed on the east by Perrault's colonnade (1667–70); the Grande Galerie runs west to the Tuileries. The court has left; academies and artists fill it.

landmarks.summary: Philippe Auguste's riverside fortress, rebuilt by Francis I and his successors as the royal palace; by 1789 the vast Cour Carrée, mostly empty of kings.
details: The castle of about 1190–1202 was a square of about 78 by 72 m with corner and gate towers round a round keep 15 m across and 30 m high. Charles V gave it lodgings and a library. In 1546 Pierre Lescot began the new palace; Lemercier and Le Vau quadrupled his court in the 17th century, and Perrault's colonnade closed it on the east.

The miniature shows each stage at the size of the Cour Carrée: the medieval castle occupied its south-west quarter, which is where the fortress sits in the 1250 model. Ornament, the dormers and the courtyard sculpture are simplified.

landmarks.name: Tuileries Palace

valois-1550.note: Tile kilns (tuileries) and gardens outside the wall. Catherine de' Medici will begin a palace here in 1564 to Philibert de l'Orme's design.

louis-1789.note: Long empty while the court lived at Versailles; Louis XVI is brought here by the crowd in October 1789. Le Nôtre's gardens run west to the Place Louis XV.

landmarks.summary: The long palace closing the west end of the Louvre, begun for Catherine de' Medici in 1564, facing Le Nôtre's gardens.
details: Philibert de l'Orme began it in 1564 for the queen mother; Jean Bullant, then Henri IV's architects added pavilions, and Le Vau and d'Orbay rebuilt it for Louis XIV with a central dome. The Pavillon de Flore at its south end joins the Grande Galerie of the Louvre. It burned in 1871 and was demolished in 1883.
The miniature shows the 270 m front with its central domed pavilion, the end pavilions of Flore and Marsan and the high slate roofs. Its garden facade faced west over the parterres.

landmarks.name: Grande Galerie of the Louvre

valois-1550.note: The river bank below the Louvre, outside the wall of Charles V. Henri IV's gallery will be built along it in 1595–1610.

louis-1789.note: The longest room in Europe, its upper floor planned as a public museum since the 1770s; below it, Henri IV lodged artists and craftsmen, and the royal mint and press worked.

landmarks.summary: Henri IV's riverside gallery (1595–1610), about 450 m long, joining the Louvre to the Tuileries along the Seine.
details: Built for Henri IV as the Grand Dessein, it let the king pass from the Louvre to the Tuileries above the street and outside the city wall. Its ground floor housed artists' and craftsmen's lodgings; the long upper room held the plan-reliefs of fortified towns until 1777, and became the main gallery of the Louvre museum in 1793.
The miniature shows the eastern half of the gallery along the quay, with its dormers and the arched windows of the ground floor; its western half continues off the model to the Pavillon de Flore.

landmarks.name: Grand Châtelet

lutetia-200.note: The right-bank landing of the Roman road north; the bridge then crossed further east.

capetian-1000.note: In 885 a timber tower here held the bridgehead against the Vikings. Louis VI rebuilt it in stone about 1130; around 1000 it was still an earth and timber fort.

philippe-1250.note: The seat of the king's provost of Paris: courts, the prison and, below, the street through its vaulted passage onto the Grand Pont.

valois-1550.note: The provost's court and prison, the morgue where the drowned from the Seine are laid out, and the standard measures of the city.

louis-1789.note: Enlarged in 1684; still the criminal court and prison of Paris. It will be pulled down in 1802.

landmarks.summary: The fortress at the right-bank end of the Grand Pont: the seat of the king's provost, its courts and one of the most dreaded prisons in Paris.
details: It began as a timber tower guarding the bridge, rebuilt in stone under Louis VI about 1130 and enlarged in the 14th century and again in 1684. The rue Saint-Denis ran through its vaulted passage. Inside were the provost's tribunal and the prison, with cells ranging from paying rooms to the pit called 'la Fin d'aise'.

The miniature shows the tower-flanked gate facing the bridge, the round towers with slate cones, the courtyard ranges and the vaulted street passage. Its exact plan before the 1684 rebuilding is uncertain.

landmarks.name: The Bastille

philippe-1250.note: Fields and vineyards outside the city on the road to the abbey of Saint-Antoine.

valois-1550.note: The bastide of the Porte Saint-Antoine, now a fortress with a bastion added on the east (1553). It guards the road and the Hôtel Saint-Pol and serves as a state prison and treasury.

louis-1789.note: A state prison holding seven men on 14 July 1789, when the crowd took it; its demolition began the next day.

landmarks.summary: The eight-towered fortress at the east gate of Paris, built 1370–83, which became the royal state prison and was stormed on 14 July 1789.
details: Begun in 1370 by the provost Hugues Aubriot for Charles V as the bastide guarding the Porte Saint-Antoine, it was a rectangle of eight round towers about 24 m high joined by walls of the same height, round two courts, behind a deep ditch. Richelieu made it a state prison; Voltaire was held here twice.

The miniature shows the eight towers and curtains with their crenellated walk, the two courts and the ditch. It leaves out the bastion and outer courts; the ring of towers and the walls of equal height are well documented.

landmarks.name: The Temple

capetian-1000.note: Marshland. The Knights Templar settled north of the city in the 1140s and began to drain and wall their enclosure.

philippe-1250.note: The Templars' fortified house, banker to the king: the round church, the old tower of Caesar, and the great keep being built (finished by about 1265).

valois-1550.note: Since the Templars' fall (1307–14) the house of the Knights Hospitaller; its walled enclosure is a refuge where debtors and artisans outside the guilds live free of the city's rules.

louis-1789.note: The Grand Prior's palace (1667) stands beside the old keep; in August 1792 Louis XVI and his family will be imprisoned in the tower.

landmarks.summary: The fortified headquarters of the Knights Templar north of the city, with its great keep and round church; later the Hospitallers' priory and the last prison of Louis XVI.
details: The Templars kept the royal treasury here in the 13th century. The great keep, about 50 m high with four corner turrets, was built in the mid-13th century; beside it stood the round church of the Holy Sepulchre type. After the Order's suppression the enclosure passed to the Hospitallers. Napoleon had the keep pulled down in 1808.

The miniature shows the square keep with its four round turrets and slate roofs, the smaller tower, the rotunda church and a stretch of the crenellated enclosure wall. The enclosure itself, about 6 hectares, is shown only in part.
landmarks.function: Templar house, then Hospitaller priory and prison

landmarks.name: Saint-Germain-des-Prés

lutetia-200.note: Open fields and meadows west of the town along the road to the west.

capetian-1000.note: The abbey of Childebert (founded 558), burned by the Vikings, is being rebuilt by Abbot Morard: the west tower-porch dates from about 990–1000.

philippe-1250.note: The Gothic choir (consecrated 1163) with its early flying buttresses; Pierre de Montreuil is building the Lady Chapel and refectory. The abbey rules its own bourg and fair.

valois-1550.note: The walled abbey, its ditches dug in the Hundred Years War, stands among the houses of a growing faubourg; its fair draws all Paris each spring.

louis-1789.note: A great Benedictine house of scholars (the Maurists), its library one of the finest in Europe. The abbey will be suppressed in 1790 and its library burn in 1794.

landmarks.summary: The Benedictine abbey 'of the meadows' west of the city, with the oldest church tower in Paris (about 1000) and an early Gothic choir.
details: Founded by King Childebert I in 558 to hold relics of Saint Vincent, it took the name of Bishop Germain, buried here in 576. The Romanesque nave and west tower date from about 1000; the choir, with some of the first flying buttresses, was consecrated by Pope Alexander III in 1163. The abbey's bourg and fair grew into the faubourg Saint-Germain.
The miniature shows the west tower with its spire, the Romanesque nave, the two towers flanking the choir (pulled down in 1822) and the Gothic apse. The cloister and abbey buildings are left out.

landmarks.name: Abbey of Sainte-Geneviève

lutetia-200.note: Houses and gardens on the summit of Mons Lucotitius above the forum. Clovis will found a church of the Holy Apostles here about 502, where Geneviève is buried.

capetian-1000.note: The canons' church rebuilt after the Viking raids, with its Romanesque bell tower (later the Tour Clovis), the shrine of the city's patron saint and its own walled bourg.

philippe-1250.note: The abbey of the Augustinian canons where Abelard taught on the hill: its school rivals Notre-Dame's, and its abbot shares authority over the University.

valois-1550.note: The great abbey on the summit, its tower heightened in Gothic style; Geneviève's shrine is carried in procession to Notre-Dame in times of flood or plague.

louis-1789.name: Sainte-Geneviève (the Panthéon)
louis-1789.note: Soufflot's new church (begun 1757), its dome finished in 1790; the old abbey church still stands beside it. In 1791 it will become the Panthéon, a mausoleum of great men.

landmarks.summary: The abbey on the summit of the Montagne, built over the tomb of Paris's patron saint, replaced in the 18th century by Soufflot's domed church, the Panthéon.
details: Clovis and Clotilde founded a church of the Holy Apostles here about 502; Geneviève, who had rallied the city against Attila in 451, was buried in it. Rebuilt after 857, it became an abbey of canons regular in 1148. Louis XV vowed a new church in 1744; Soufflot's design, a Greek cross with a dome on columns, was built 1757–90.

The abbey model shows the church with its tall west tower, cloister and buildings; the 1789 model shows the Panthéon's portico of Corinthian columns and its three-shelled dome. The medieval plan is partly reconstructed.

landmarks.name: The Sorbonne

philippe-1250.note: Houses on the rue Coupe-Gueule. In 1257 Robert de Sorbon, chaplain to Louis IX, will buy them to found a college for poor students of theology.

valois-1550.name: Collège de Sorbonne
valois-1550.note: The theology college whose doctors judge heresy for all France; France's first printing press worked here from 1470. Its plain Gothic buildings stand round a court with a chapel.

louis-1789.note: Rebuilt by Lemercier for Cardinal Richelieu (1626–42), with the domed chapel where Richelieu lies buried; the faculty of theology still meets here.

landmarks.summary: The theology college founded by Robert de Sorbon in 1257, which gave its name to the University of Paris; rebuilt by Richelieu with a domed chapel.
details: The college began with sixteen poor masters reading theology and grew into the faculty's heart; its doctors condemned Luther in 1521. The first press in France was set up here in 1470 by three German printers invited by Guillaume Fichet and Johann Heynlin. Richelieu, its provisor, rebuilt it entirely from 1626.

The 1550 model shows a court of plain gabled ranges with a small chapel; the 1789 model shows Lemercier's court and the chapel facing west, with its dome and lantern. The medieval layout is reconstructed.

landmarks.name: Hôtel de Ville

philippe-1250.note: Houses on the Place de Grève. The merchants of the water meet at the Parloir aux Bourgeois; in 1357 Étienne Marcel will buy the Maison aux Piliers here for the city.

valois-1550.note: Begun in 1533 to Domenico da Cortona's design; the southern half is rising beside the old Maison aux Piliers, which still serves. It will not be finished until 1628.

louis-1789.note: The provost of the merchants and the échevins govern from here; on 13–14 July 1789 the electors of Paris meet in it and the new National Guard forms.

landmarks.summary: The town hall of Paris on the Place de Grève, a Renaissance palace begun in 1533 beside the city's old Maison aux Piliers.
details: The city's government, led by the provost of the merchants, moved to the Maison aux Piliers on the Grève in 1357. Francis I had it rebuilt in the Italian manner from 1533, to a design by Domenico da Cortona; work dragged on until 1628. The square in front, the Grève, was the city's port, hiring place and scaffold. It burned in 1871 and was rebuilt.

The 1789 model shows the long front with its central belfry and end pavilions under high slate roofs; the 1550 model shows the half-built new wing beside the old arcaded house. Details of the 1550 work are uncertain.

landmarks.name: Pont Notre-Dame

philippe-1250.note: Only the Planches de Mibray, a plank footbridge, crossed the north arm here, on the line of the Roman Grand Pont.

valois-1550.note: The stone bridge of 1500–1512, rebuilt after the timber bridge collapsed in 1499: five arches carrying two rows of identical brick-and-stone houses, numbered, the city's showpiece.

louis-1789.note: Its houses were pulled down in 1786 by royal order to let air and light along the river; a water pump stands under one arch.

landmarks.summary: The bridge of houses: rebuilt in stone in 1500–1512 with two rows of uniform houses, the first numbered street in Paris.
details: A timber bridge of 1413 here fell into the Seine on 25 October 1499, with its houses. The city rebuilt it in stone with five arches and some sixty-odd houses of uniform design, numbered, their rents paying for the bridge. Royal entries crossed it on the way to Notre-Dame. The houses were demolished in 1786.
The 1550 model shows the five arches with cutwaters and the double row of gabled houses meeting over the roadway; the 1789 model shows the bare bridge. The house fronts are simplified.

landmarks.name: Pont au Change

capetian-1000.note: The Grand Pont, rebuilt here in the 9th century, crosses on piers with water mills between them; the changers already work on it by the 12th century.

philippe-1250.name: Grand Pont (Pont aux Changeurs)
philippe-1250.note: The main bridge of Paris, lined with the booths and houses of money-changers and goldsmiths, with mills beneath. Whether it was then of stone or timber is uncertain.

valois-1550.note: A timber bridge rebuilt after the flood of 1296 and many times since, with houses on both sides; changers and goldsmiths by royal statute.

louis-1789.note: Rebuilt in stone in 1639–47 after the fire of 1621, with houses that were pulled down in 1786–88; the open bridge now shows the Châtelet and the Palace.

landmarks.summary: The Grand Pont of medieval Paris, renamed for the money-changers who did business on it under royal privilege; from the Châtelet to the Palace.
details: Bridges stood here from the 9th century. Louis VII fixed the changers on the Grand Pont in 1141, and goldsmiths shared it; mills turned between its piers. Swept away in 1296, burned in 1621, it was rebuilt in stone in 1639–47, 32 m wide to carry two rows of houses, which were demolished in 1786–88.

The medieval model shows a timber bridge on pile piers carrying two rows of narrow gabled houses over a central street; the 1789 model shows the stone bridge of seven arches. How the 13th-century bridge was built is unknown.

landmarks.name: Pont Neuf

valois-1550.note: Open river and the small islands off the Cité's point. Henri III will lay the first stone of a new bridge in 1578; Henri IV will open it in 1607.

louis-1789.note: The busiest street of Paris: hawkers, tooth-pullers, booksellers and recruiting sergeants on its half-moon bays, the bronze Henri IV at the centre and the Samaritaine pump on the north side.

landmarks.summary: The 'new bridge' of 1578–1607 across the point of the Cité: the first Paris bridge without houses, with pavements, and the city's favourite promenade.
details: Begun by Henri III and finished by Henri IV, it crosses both arms in twelve arches, joined by the newly made Place Dauphine and the point of the island. It had raised pavements and semicircular bays over every pier, but no houses, so that the king could see the Louvre. The Samaritaine pump (1608) supplied the palaces.

The miniature shows the two spans with their half-moon bays, the cornice of carved masks, the equestrian statue of Henri IV (1614) on the point and the Samaritaine pump house on the downstream side of the north span.

landmarks.name: Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie

philippe-1250.note: The parish church of the butchers' quarter by the Grande Boucherie, a starting point for pilgrims bound for Compostela.

valois-1550.note: Rebuilt in flamboyant Gothic; the bell tower of 1509–23, 58 m high, paid for by the rich butchers, is the tallest in the Ville.

louis-1789.note: Still a busy parish; the church will be sold in 1797 and pulled down, leaving only the tower.

landmarks.summary: The butchers' parish church by the Châtelet, whose flamboyant Gothic bell tower (1509–23) survives as the Tour Saint-Jacques.
details: A parish church existed here by the 12th century, serving the butchers' guild of the Grande Boucherie next door; Nicolas Flamel, the scrivener later famed as an alchemist, was a parishioner. The church was rebuilt in the 15th and 16th centuries and crowned with its tower in 1509–23. It was demolished after 1797; the tower was saved.
The 1550 model shows the church with its tall square tower and corner pinnacles at the west end; the 1250 model a smaller church with a simple belfry. The church plan is reconstructed from old views.

landmarks.name: Les Halles

capetian-1000.note: The Champeaux, the 'little fields' outside the town. Louis VI moved a market here about 1137, and Philippe Auguste built the first two halls in 1183.

philippe-1250.note: Two great covered halls for the cloth-sellers and weavers, with stalls round them and a wall with gates; trades from outside the city sell here on set days.

valois-1550.note: Francis I has begun rebuilding the halls (from 1543), with the arcaded 'piliers' houses round them; the pillory stands in the market square.

louis-1789.note: A permanent market for all Paris: fish, grain, cloth, vegetables, the pillory, the forts des Halles (porters) and the fishwives of the Halles.

landmarks.summary: The central market of Paris, where Philippe Auguste built two covered halls in 1183; the 'belly of Paris' until 1969.
details: Louis VI moved a market to the Champeaux about 1137; Philippe Auguste built two halls in 1183 for the drapers and weavers and walled the site. More halls followed for each trade and for merchants of other towns. Francis I's rebuilding from 1543 surrounded them with arcaded houses. The market moved to Rungis in 1969.

The miniature shows long timber halls under steep roofs, open-sided stalls, a walled yard and the octagonal pillory tower. The number and layout of the halls changed constantly; this is a simplified reconstruction.

landmarks.name: Cemetery of the Holy Innocents

capetian-1000.note: A burial ground since Merovingian times round the small church of the Holy Innocents. Philippe Auguste will wall it in 1186.

philippe-1250.note: The walled cemetery of twenty parishes and the Hôtel-Dieu, with the church at its north-east corner and the open pits for the poor.

valois-1550.note: Arcaded charnel houses stacked with bones line the walls, painted with the Danse Macabre (1424); Jean Goujon's new fountain (1549) stands at the corner of the rue Saint-Denis.

louis-1789.name: Marché des Innocents
louis-1789.note: Closed in 1780 after cellars collapsed into the pits; the bones went to the catacombs in 1785–87. Goujon's fountain, moved to the centre, waters a new vegetable market.

landmarks.summary: The great cemetery of medieval Paris, with its charnel arcades and Danse Macabre; closed in 1780 and turned into a market round Goujon's Fountain of the Innocents.
details: For centuries most Parisians who died were buried here, in mass graves for the poor; bones were cleared into the galleries of charnel houses along the walls. The 1424 Danse Macabre painted under the arcades was famous across Europe. Yet it was also a public place of shops, scribes and lovers' meetings. In 1780 its smell and seepage closed it.

The miniatures show the walled field with arcaded charnels, the church and, from 1549, the fountain; the 1789 model shows the market square with the fountain in the middle. The charnels' extent is reconstructed.

landmarks.name: Baths and Hôtel de Cluny

lutetia-200.name: North Baths (Thermes de Cluny)
lutetia-200.note: The largest baths of Lutetia, built about 200: frigidarium, tepidarium and caldarium in a row, with the palaestra and shops, fed by the aqueduct from Wissous.

capetian-1000.name: Ruined baths
capetian-1000.note: The baths, wrecked in the late 3rd century, stand roofless except for the vaulted frigidarium, overgrown and quarried.

philippe-1250.name: Ruined baths
philippe-1250.note: Ruins in gardens among the houses of the University; the abbots of Cluny will buy the site about 1330.

valois-1550.note: The town house of the abbots of Cluny, built about 1485–1510 by Jacques d'Amboise, with its flamboyant chapel; the Roman frigidarium still stands beside it, a garden on its vault.

louis-1789.note: The hôtel is let out; the astronomer Messier has his observatory in its tower. The frigidarium is a cooper's workshop.

landmarks.summary: Lutetia's great baths, whose 14 m vaulted cold room still stands, and the late Gothic town house of the abbots of Cluny built beside it.
details: The North Baths, the biggest of Lutetia's three, were built about 200 CE; the frigidarium, 21 by 11 m under a ribbed vault 14 m high, survived because its vault was so solid. The abbots of Cluny bought the site in the 14th century, and Jacques d'Amboise built their hôtel round a court about 1485–1510.

The Roman model reconstructs the bath block, palaestra and shops; the medieval one shows the surviving frigidarium amid ruined walls; the later one the hôtel with its stair tower and dormers beside the Roman hall.

landmarks.name: Arena of Lutetia

lutetia-200.note: Built in the late 1st century: an amphitheatre with a stage on one side, for games, beast hunts and plays, holding perhaps 15,000 people, more than lived in the town.

capetian-1000.note: Gone: quarried for the wall of the Cité about 300, then buried. Only the name of the Clos des Arènes recalled it; it was rediscovered in 1869.

landmarks.summary: Lutetia's amphitheatre-theatre of the late 1st century on the eastern slope of the hill: an oval arena with tiers on three sides and a stage on the fourth.
details: A Gallo-Roman type that mixes amphitheatre and theatre: an arena about 52 by 46 m, tiers in a horseshoe for perhaps 15,000 spectators, and a stage building with nine niches on the east. Stones from it went into the late Roman wall. It was found when the rue Monge was cut in 1869, saved by a campaign led by Victor Hugo.
The miniature shows the arena, the tiered cavea, the stage wall with its niches and the entrances. The height of the tiers and the stage are reconstructed.

landmarks.name: Forum of Lutetia

lutetia-200.note: The civic centre astride the line of the rue Soufflot: a temple at the west end of a colonnaded square, shops along the sides, a basilica at the east end on the cardo.

capetian-1000.note: Gone: its stones went into the wall of the Cité. Vineyards and the clos of the left bank cover the site.

landmarks.summary: The forum of Lutetia on the shoulder of the hill, about 180 by 90 m: temple, porticoes with shops and a basilica, under today's rue Soufflot.
details: Excavated in pieces since the 19th century, it measured about 178 by 89 m. A temple stood in a colonnaded court at the west end; the public square in the middle was lined by double porticoes with shops behind; the basilica closed the east end along the cardo (rue Saint-Jacques). It was built in the 1st century CE.
The miniature shows the temple on its podium, the porticoed square and shops and the basilica. Heights and the temple's order are reconstructed by analogy with other Gallic forums.

landmarks.name: Saint-Eustache

philippe-1250.note: A chapel of Saint Agnes (1213), raised to a parish dedicated to Saint Eustace in 1223, serving the quarter of the Halles.

valois-1550.note: The great new church begun in 1532: Gothic in plan and height, Renaissance in its detail. The east end is rising beside the old church; it will be finished in 1637.

louis-1789.note: Complete, with a new classical west front (1754–88) whose south tower was never finished. Richelieu, Molière and Louis XIV were baptised or married in its parish.

landmarks.summary: The parish church of the Halles, begun in 1532: a Gothic cathedral-sized body dressed in Renaissance ornament, with a classical west front added in the 18th century.
details: The market parish built it on the scale of Notre-Dame: 105 m long, five aisles, vaults 33 m high, but with Corinthian pilasters and round arches. Work began in 1532 and lasted until 1637. A new west front by Mansart de Jouy and Moreau-Desproux replaced the unfinished old one from 1754.

The 1789 model shows the nave and transept with flying buttresses, the apse and the classical front with its one finished tower; the 1550 model shows the choir under construction with the nave not yet begun.

landmarks.name: Place Royale (Place des Vosges)

valois-1550.note: The royal Hôtel des Tournelles and its gardens. Henri II died here after his jousting wound of 1559, and Catherine de' Medici had it demolished.

louis-1789.note: The square of the Marais nobility, with Louis XIII on horseback in the railed garden; the fashionable world has moved west, but the arcades still hold the salons of old families.

landmarks.summary: Henri IV's square of 1605–12: thirty-six matching houses of brick and stone over arcades round a garden, the first planned residential square in Paris.
details: Henri IV laid it out on the site of the Tournelles to house a silk works and then the court nobility; it was inaugurated in 1612 with the celebrations for Louis XIII's betrothal. Nine houses on each side, each of red brick with stone dressings and steep slate roofs, stand over a continuous arcade; the taller King's and Queen's pavilions face each other.
The miniature shows the four ranges with their arcades and separate roofs, the two taller pavilions, the garden with its railings and the equestrian statue of Louis XIII (1639).

landmarks.name: Tour de Nesle

capetian-1000.note: River bank meadows of the abbey of Saint-Germain; the Pré-aux-Clercs, the students' playing field, lies just west.

philippe-1250.note: The round tower where Philippe Auguste's left-bank wall meets the Seine; a chain stretched to the Louvre's Tour du Coin could close the river at night.

valois-1550.note: Attached to the Hôtel de Nesle, Benvenuto Cellini's workshop under Francis I; legend says Philip IV's daughters-in-law met their lovers here (the scandal of 1314).

louis-1789.note: Demolished in 1665 for Mazarin's Collège des Quatre-Nations, whose domed chapel now stands here facing the Louvre.

landmarks.summary: The 25 m round tower that ended Philippe Auguste's wall on the left bank, facing the Louvre across the Seine; the scene of a famous royal scandal and legend.
details: Built about 1200 as the river-end tower of the left-bank wall, with a stair turret rising above it. In 1314 the daughters-in-law of Philip the Fair were accused of adultery with two knights; legend, embroidered by Brantôme and Alexandre Dumas, made the tower a place of murder. It was pulled down in 1665.
The miniature shows the tall round tower with its crenellated top and slate cone, the slimmer stair turret and a stub of the wall running inland. Heights follow old engravings.

landmarks.name: Wall of Philippe Auguste (Saint-Paul)

capetian-1000.note: Open land east of the bourg of Saint-Gervais. The wall will be built here about 1190–1210.

philippe-1250.note: New: a stone wall 6 to 8 m high with a walk behind its battlements and round towers every 60–70 m, running down to the Seine at the Tour Barbeau.

valois-1550.note: Redundant since the wall of Charles V; houses lean against it on both sides and the towers are let as dwellings and workshops.

louis-1789.note: Swallowed by houses, it survives inside their walls; this stretch along the rue des Jardins-Saint-Paul was uncovered again in 1946.

landmarks.summary: The longest surviving stretch of Philippe Auguste's wall of about 1190–1215, with two of its round towers, running down toward the Seine in the Saint-Paul quarter.
details: Philippe Auguste ordered the wall in 1190 before leaving on crusade. About 5.3 km round, 2.5 to 3 m thick at the base and 6 to 8 m high, it had some 77 towers and a dozen gates. It had no ditch on the right bank at first. Inside it the fields filled with houses within a century.
The miniature shows a 110 m run of crenellated wall with a wall-walk and two round towers, as at the rue des Jardins-Saint-Paul.

spots.name: Pillar of the Boatmen
spots.summary: A carved stone pillar set up by the boatmen's guild of the Parisii under Tiberius, honouring Jupiter, Gaulish gods and Roman gods side by side, at the east end of the island.
details: Its inscription reads that the nautae Parisiaci raised it to Jupiter Optimus Maximus in the reign of Tiberius (14–37 CE). Its blocks show Jupiter, Vulcan, Castor and Pollux beside the Gaulish Esus cutting a tree, the bull with three cranes and the horned Cernunnos. Found under Notre-Dame's choir in 1711, it is the oldest monument of Paris.

vignettes.text: A boat-master lays a little bronze coin and a cake at the foot of the pillar before casting off downstream with a cargo of wine jars for the coast.
Members of the guild, in hooded cloaks, gather here to settle a dispute over a lost cargo; the priest reads the names carved on the stones.
Swallows over the river. The carved bull and the three cranes catch the last light; you can hear the rush of the north arm under the bridge.

spots.name: Eastern Baths
spots.summary: A smaller public bath east of the cardo, under today's Collège de France: a neighbourhood bath for the people of the hillside streets.
details: Lutetia had at least three public baths: the North (Cluny) Baths, the Forum Baths and these Eastern Baths, found under the Collège de France. Walls of small limestone blocks banded with brick, hypocausts and a cold pool have been traced. Water came by the aqueduct from Wissous, which also served private houses.
Julian, who wintered here, wrote that the people of Lutetia drank the river water, which was clear and good to look at.

vignettes.text: The furnace slave rakes the ashes and feeds the fire with oak from the hill; steam starts to curl from the vents.
Afternoon is the busy hour: shopkeepers from the cardo, a potter with clay still on his arms, two veterans comparing scars in the warm room.
Women's hour is over; the attendant scrapes oil and grime off the last bather's back with a strigil while the lamps are lit.

spots.name: Cloister school of Notre-Dame
spots.summary: The canons' school in the cloister north of the cathedral, where Abelard drew students from all Europe about 1115 and where the chancellor licensed every master in Paris.
details: In the early 12th century masters taught in the cloister of the cathedral and on the Montagne; students came from England, Germany and Italy. Abelard, the most famous, lodged with the canon Fulbert and fell in love with his niece Héloïse; it ended in his castration. The chancellor of Notre-Dame kept the right to grant the licence to teach.

vignettes.text: Students in black wrap themselves against the cold, sitting on the cloister floor with wax tablets, waiting for the master after matins.
The master reads a line of Boethius, then sets yes against no: 'Sic et non'. Fifty voices take sides.
Lamps behind the canons' shutters; in a house on the quay a tutor is not teaching his pupil grammar.

philippe-1250.note: Most masters have moved to the left bank, but the chancellor still grants licences here; the University fights him over it.

spots.name: Synagogue of the rue de la Juiverie
spots.summary: The synagogue of the Jews of Paris in the street named after them on the Cité, until Philippe Auguste expelled them in 1182 and gave it to the Church.
details: A Jewish community lived on the Cité and on the right bank from at least the 11th century; the rue de la Juiverie ran across the island from the Petit Pont. After the expulsion of 1182 the synagogue probably became the church of Sainte-Madeleine-en-la-Cité. Jews were readmitted in 1198 and expelled again in 1306 and 1394.

vignettes.text: Men in cloaks with the round badge not yet imposed go in for the morning prayer; a moneylender opens his shutter on the street outside.
A scholar argues a passage of Rashi's new commentary, brought from Troyes, with the rabbi; children chant the alphabet in the next room.
Friday dusk: lamps lit for the Sabbath in the houses of the street, the shops shut, the noise of the bridge carts beyond.

spots.name: Port de Grève
spots.summary: The great river port of Paris on the gravel shore (grève) of the right bank: wine, grain, wood and hay unloaded from barges under the eye of the merchants of the water.
details: The hanse of the marchands de l'eau held the monopoly of river trade into Paris from the 12th century; goods coming upstream had to be sold through a Paris merchant. Porters, measurers and criers worked the shore. Separate ports specialised: wine and grain at the Grève, firewood further up, hay at the Port au Foin.

vignettes.text: Barges of Burgundy wine nose onto the gravel; sworn measurers count casks while porters with leather hoods roll them up the planks.
A crier of the hanse calls the price of grain; a merchant from Rouen, forbidden to sell direct, haggles with his Paris partner.
Woodmen stack the last logs; a boatman sleeps under a tarpaulin to guard his load from thieves.

louis-1789.note: Still the port for wood, wine and grain; the quays are being stone-faced, and the floating laundries moor nearby.

spots.name: Place de Grève
spots.summary: The sloping square before the Hôtel de Ville: the city's hiring place, its bonfire ground on Saint John's Eve and, for six centuries, its place of execution.
details: Unemployed workmen gathered here each morning to be hired: 'faire grève' first meant to wait for work here, later to strike. Executions drew huge crowds: the regicide Ravaillac was torn apart by horses here in 1610, Damiens in 1757. On Saint John's Eve the city lit a great bonfire, the king sometimes setting the torch.

vignettes.text: Masons and labourers stand about the square with their tools, waiting for a master builder to come down and hire them for the day.
A gallows has gone up overnight. The crowd fills the windows round the square; vendors sell wafers and wine.
Saint John's Eve: a tree-high bonfire, a sack of live cats hung over it, as was the custom until the 17th century; the whole Grève shouts.

spots.name: Hôtel-Dieu
spots.summary: The cathedral's hospital on the river beside the parvis, open to every sick and poor person in Paris, run by Augustinian nuns and brothers.
details: Tradition dates it to Bishop Landry in the 7th century. Rebuilt in the 12th and 13th centuries, it had long wards on the south arm of the Seine, later spanning it. Patients often lay two, three or more to a bed; the sisters washed the linen in the river. Fires in 1737 and 1772 ravaged it.

vignettes.text: The sisters change the straw, carry out the night's dead to the cart for the Innocents and wash sheets at the river steps.
Bread, broth and wine are carried down the long ward; a canon of Notre-Dame hears confessions from bed to bed.
Lamps along the ward; a novice watches over a fever case while the river slaps against the foundations below.

louis-1789.note: Some 2,500 patients, often four to a bed; Tenon's report of 1788 calls it the worst hospital in Europe and urges it be moved.

spots.name: Rue du Fouarre
spots.summary: The 'street of straw' near the place Maubert, where the masters of the Arts faculty rented rooms and their students sat on straw on the floor to hear lectures.
details: The four 'nations' of the Arts faculty (French, Picard, Norman and English-German) held their schools here; students sat on bundles of straw (fouarre). Dante put the philosopher Siger of Brabant here, 'reading in the Street of Straw'. Lectures began at dawn with the reading of a text and ended in disputations.

vignettes.text: Before light, a master in a black gown reads Aristotle's Logic aloud in Latin; you sit on straw with your feet freezing, copying as fast as you can.
Disputation: a bachelor defends a thesis on universals against all comers. The straw is kicked about; a beadle calls for order.
The street empties into the taverns of the Maubert. Students of the Picard nation sing; the watch passes without looking in.

valois-1550.note: Still the street of the Arts faculty, but teaching has moved inside the colleges; the old schools are let to the nations for ceremonies.

spots.name: Changers and goldsmiths of the Grand Pont
spots.summary: The money-changers' booths on the Grand Pont, fixed there by Louis VII in 1141, side by side with the goldsmiths' shops: the money market of medieval Paris.
details: Coins of Tours, Paris, England and Italy circulated side by side, and changers weighed and exchanged them at fixed booths on the bridge, their scales on the counter. Goldsmiths, under strict statutes, worked and sold their plate here and on the quay. Royal entries passed between their shops, hung with tapestries.

vignettes.text: Shutters drop to become counters; a changer sets his scales and stacks of deniers parisis beside the coins of Tours.
A Lombard merchant and an English wool buyer argue the rate for an Italian florin while the goldsmith next door taps at a chalice.
A royal sergeant checks the goldsmiths' marks; the changers count up and lock their chests in the house above the shop.

louis-1789.name: Quai des Orfèvres
louis-1789.note: The houses on the bridge are gone; the goldsmiths now work along the quai des Orfèvres and the place Dauphine.

spots.name: Grande Boucherie
spots.summary: The butchers' hall in front of the Grand Châtelet, held by a closed guild of a few families, with slaughterhouses and tanneries in the streets round about.
details: The Grande Boucherie belonged to some twenty hereditary families who controlled the meat trade of the right bank; the stalls passed from father to son. Animals were slaughtered behind the stalls, the blood running down to the Seine. The butchers' wealth paid for the tower of Saint-Jacques; their street gangs, the Cabochiens, terrorised Paris in 1413.

vignettes.text: Oxen driven down the rue Saint-Denis bellow outside the slaughter yards; lanterns, cleavers, the smell of blood and straw.
Cooks from the great houses choose joints at the stalls; a dog makes off with a scrap and is chased into the Châtelet passage.
Boys sluice the blood toward the river; tallow-chandlers collect fat in buckets for their candles.

spots.name: Pillory of the Halles
spots.summary: The octagonal tower in the market where fraudulent traders, blasphemers and bankrupts were displayed, turning on a wheel so the whole crowd could see them.
details: The pillory was a small stone tower with a revolving wooden platform on top, in which the condemned stood with head and hands locked in a board; every half hour they were turned to face a new side of the market. Market fraud, false weights and blasphemy earned a turn there; the crowd threw mud and rotten produce.

vignettes.text: A baker caught selling short loaves is turned on the wheel, the loaves hung round his neck; fishwives shout at him.
Noon: the market at its height, carts jammed round the tower, a crier reading a sentence over the noise.
The sergeants unlock the board; the man limps off, splashed with cabbage, while the stalls pack up.

spots.name: Étuves of the rue des Vieilles-Étuves
spots.summary: Public steam baths (étuves), some thirty of them in 13th-century Paris, where men and women bathed on separate days; their criers announced each morning that the water was hot.
details: The statutes of the étuveurs in Étienne Boileau's Livre des métiers forbade crying the baths before daylight, because thieves used it as a pretext, and forbade keeping prostitutes. A bath in a wooden tub or the steam room cost a few deniers. Fear of plague and syphilis emptied the bathhouses in the 16th century.

vignettes.text: As soon as it is light the crier walks the street: 'Seigneurs, venez vous baigner et étuver, les bains sont chauds, c'est sans mentir!'
Steam, wooden tubs under linen canopies, a barber shaving a customer, a servant bringing wine and wafers.
The fires are banked; the bath-keeper's wife counts the takings, wary of a sergeant who has heard rumours about the back rooms.

valois-1550.note: Few remain: preachers denounce them, and fear of the 'great pox' and the plague has closed most.

spots.name: Taverne de la Pomme de Pin
spots.summary: The most famous tavern of old Paris, on the Cité near the Madeleine church, named in Villon's Testament and later haunted by Rabelais and the poets of the Pléiade.
details: Villon bequeathed jokes to its owner, Robin Turgis, in 1461. A century later Rabelais mentions it among the good taverns of Paris, and Ronsard and his friends drank here. Taverns sold wine by the pot under the sign of a pine cone or a bush; a crier of wine stood at the door.

vignettes.text: A wine crier with a jug and a cup offers tastes at the door; clerks of the Palais come in for a quick pot between hearings.
Two young poets argue over the sonnet, Greek and French; the landlord chalks their score on the wall.
Curfew has rung at Notre-Dame, but the back room still sings; the watch knocks and is given a pot to go away.

spots.name: Press of the Soleil d'Or, rue Saint-Jacques
spots.summary: The printing house at the sign of the Golden Sun, where Ulrich Gering moved the first Paris press from the Sorbonne in 1473: the start of the street of printers and booksellers.
details: Gering, Crantz and Friburger came from Germany in 1470 to print in the Sorbonne; in 1473 they set up as independent printers in the rue Saint-Jacques. By the 16th century the street was lined with presses and bookshops under the University's oversight, among them the Estiennes. Royal censorship weighed on them after the Affair of the Placards (1534).

vignettes.text: Apprentices ink the forme with leather balls; the pressman pulls the bar, the platen thumps down, and another sheet of Cicero comes up wet.
A regent of the Collège de Navarre checks proofs at the counter; students thumb cheap grammars they cannot afford.
The sheets hang drying on lines across the workshop; the master locks the shop, wary of the inspectors looking for Protestant books.

louis-1789.note: The rue Saint-Jacques is still the booksellers' street; in 1789 its presses are turning out pamphlets night and day.

spots.name: Cour des Miracles
spots.summary: The courtyard slum near the Porte Saint-Denis where, by legend, beggars who feigned blindness and sores by day were 'miraculously' cured each night.
details: Paris had several such courts; this was the largest, between the rue Saint-Denis and the rue Montorgueil. Sauval, who went in in the 17th century, described a muddy, sloping court of crumbling hovels where thieves and beggars kept their own rules. Much of its reputation is literary; La Reynie, lieutenant of police, cleared it in 1667.

vignettes.text: A man straps up a leg to look like a stump and smears his arm with flour paste and blood; his partner rehearses fits.
Children play in the mud between leaning houses; an old woman sells soup and sour wine to those back early from the churches.
The day's alms are counted round a fire, the cripples walking; strangers are not welcome.

louis-1789.note: Cleared by La Reynie's police in 1667; the courts were rebuilt as ordinary tenements.

spots.name: Foire Saint-Germain
spots.summary: The abbey's great fair, held each year from February to Easter under timber halls, where all Paris came to buy, gamble and watch puppets and rope-dancers.
details: The abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés received the right to a fair in 1482. Its covered halls, rebuilt in 1511, held some 340 stalls in streets named after trades: silks, porcelain, jewellery, pictures. Its theatres of the fair gave birth to the Opéra-Comique. A fire destroyed the halls in 1762; they were rebuilt.

vignettes.text: Merchants from Flanders and Lyon unroll silks under the great timber roof; a lady's page carries a monkey bought for her.
A crowd round the rope-dancers and a puppet show; pickpockets work the crush; dice clatter in a back booth.
Lanterns along the alleys of stalls; young noblemen, a little drunk, pick a quarrel with the abbey's guards.

spots.name: Café Procope
spots.summary: The café opened in 1686 by the Sicilian Francesco Procopio opposite the Comédie-Française: coffee, ices and the talk of Voltaire, Diderot and, in 1789, the revolutionaries.
details: Procopio sold coffee, chocolate, liqueurs and sorbets in a room of mirrors and chandeliers. The actors of the Comédie-Française, which settled across the street in 1689, and its audiences made it the literary café of Paris. The Encyclopédie was talked over here; Danton, Marat and Desmoulins came in the Revolution.

vignettes.text: A waiter pours coffee from a long-spouted pot; a journalist reads the Gazette aloud to a table that disagrees with every line.
Ices in little glasses; two playwrights wait for the reviews of last night's play and pretend not to care.
The play across the street is over; the room fills with actors and critics, and a pamphlet is passed under the table.

spots.name: Café de Foy, Palais-Royal
spots.summary: A café in the arcades of the Palais-Royal, the duc d'Orléans' garden of shops, gambling dens and brothels where the royal police could not enter; the hub of rumour in 1789.
details: The duc d'Orléans built the arcades round his garden in 1781–84 and let them out to shops and cafés. As the duke's property it was outside the police's reach, and pamphlets, speeches and gossip flowed. On 12 July 1789 Camille Desmoulins climbed on a table here and called Paris to arms.

vignettes.text: Newsmongers under the trees of the garden; a man reads the latest from Versailles to a crowd standing on chairs.
Shops under the arcades sell watches, prints and silk; a gambler comes up from a cellar with empty pockets.
The arcades are lit; women of the town walk the galleries, and in the café politics grows louder with the punch.

spots.name: Booksellers of the Pont Neuf
spots.summary: Stalls of second-hand books, songs and pamphlets on the half-moon bays of the Pont Neuf and along the quays, the ancestors of the bouquinistes.
details: Sellers of books on the Pont Neuf appear from the early 17th century; the booksellers' guild repeatedly tried to have them banned, and they were moved on and came back. Song-sellers, quacks, puppeteers and the famous tooth-puller Grand Thomas worked beside them. Mercier called the bridge the heart of Paris.

vignettes.text: A stallholder lays out battered Latin grammars and almanacs on a cloth; the Samaritaine's chimes play over the river.
Grand Thomas, in a silver-laced coat, pulls a tooth on his platform while his drummer drowns the patient's cries.
A song-seller sings the newest verses against the queen; a man in grey, a police spy, writes down the words.

spots.name: Water-carriers at the Pompe Notre-Dame
spots.summary: The water pumps of 1670 under the Pont Notre-Dame, lifting Seine water to the fountains, and the twenty thousand water-carriers who carried it up the stairs of Paris.
details: Most Parisians drank Seine water. The pump house at the Pont Notre-Dame fed public fountains; water-carriers, many of them from the Auvergne, filled two buckets on a yoke at fountains or straight from the river and sold them by the 'voie' up to the sixth floor. Mercier counts them at about twenty thousand.

vignettes.text: A queue of carriers with yokes and wooden buckets at the fountain; the pump wheel under the bridge groans and splashes.
A carrier from the Auvergne climbs six flights in the rue de la Tixéranderie for two sous a load, spilling on every landing.
The carriers drink together in a cabaret on the quay, speaking their own patois; one counts his week's coppers into a stocking.

events.title: Geneviève holds Paris against panic
events.text: As Attila's Huns swept into Gaul, the people of Paris, as Lutetia was now called, prepared to flee. A young consecrated woman, Geneviève, gathered the women to pray and told the men to stay. Attila turned south to Orléans instead. Her Life, written about 520, makes her the city's protector; her relics would be carried through the streets in every later crisis.

events.title: Julian proclaimed emperor at Lutetia
events.text: The Caesar Julian had wintered at Lutetia, 'my dear Lutetia', between campaigns on the Rhine. When Constantius II ordered his best troops east, the soldiers surrounded his palace at night and hailed him Augustus, raising him on an infantry shield. Ammianus says he resisted, then accepted. Julian later described the island town, its clear river and the vines and figs that Parisians wrapped in straw for winter.

events.title: The Vikings besiege Paris
events.text: A Danish fleet of hundreds of ships, by the monk Abbo's count, demanded passage up the Seine. Count Odo and Bishop Gozlin refused. They attacked the half-built tower at the Grand Pont's head with rams and fire. In February a flood swept away the Petit Pont and its tower fell, its twelve defenders killed. The emperor paid them to go on to Burgundy; Odo became king.

events.title: Philippe Auguste expels the Jews
events.text: The young king ordered the Jews of the royal domain to leave within three months, cancelled debts owed to them and seized their houses. The synagogue of the Cité was given to the Church, probably becoming the church of Sainte-Madeleine; houses went to the drapers and furriers. The king's chronicler Rigord presents it as piety; it was also a windfall for the treasury. Jews were let back in 1198.

events.title: The first stone of Notre-Dame
events.text: Bishop Maurice de Sully, son of a peasant, began a new cathedral east of the old Saint-Étienne, to be the largest of its day. Tradition says Pope Alexander III, in exile in France, laid the first stone. A new street, the rue Neuve-Notre-Dame, was cut to bring the stone from the quays. The choir's high altar was consecrated in 1189.

events.title: Philippe Auguste walls the right bank
events.text: Before leaving on the Third Crusade, the king ordered the burghers to enclose the right bank with a stone wall; they finished it about 1209, and the king paid for the left-bank half. It took in fields and vineyards as well as houses, and within a century they had filled up. Rigord praises the king for it; its towers and gates fixed the shape of Paris for 150 years.

events.title: The University goes on strike
events.text: A carnival brawl over a tavern bill in the faubourg Saint-Marcel ended with the queen regent's sergeants killing several students. When no redress came, the masters suspended teaching and left Paris for Orléans, Angers, Toulouse, Oxford and Cambridge. Two years later Pope Gregory IX's bull Parens scientiarum (1231) confirmed the University's right to strike and its independence.

events.title: Louis IX brings the Crown of Thorns
events.text: Louis IX bought the relic from the bankrupt Latin emperor of Constantinople, who had pawned it to Venetian bankers. The king and his brother Robert, barefoot and in plain tunics, carried it into Paris and to Notre-Dame, then to the palace chapel. The Sainte-Chapelle was built to house it; its glass tells the story of this procession.

events.title: The Sainte-Chapelle consecrated
events.text: Six years after it was begun, the palace chapel was consecrated in two ceremonies: the upper chapel by the papal legate Eudes de Châteauroux, the lower by the archbishop of Bourges. Two months later Louis IX left on crusade. The relics cost about 135,000 livres, the chapel about 40,000: the reliquary cost less than what it held.

events.title: Étienne Marcel storms the palace
events.text: With King John a prisoner in England, the provost of the merchants led some 3,000 armed Parisians into the palace and had the marshals of Champagne and Normandy cut down in front of the dauphin Charles, whose robe was splashed with their blood. Marcel put his own red-and-blue hood on the prince's head. In July Marcel was killed at the Porte Saint-Antoine; the dauphin never forgot.

events.title: The first stone of the Bastille
events.text: Hugues Aubriot, Charles V's provost of Paris, laid the first stone of a bastide to guard the Porte Saint-Antoine and the king's new residence, the Hôtel Saint-Pol. Finished about 1383, its eight towers became the anchor of the new right-bank wall. Aubriot, the story goes, was later among its first prisoners.

events.title: The Pont Notre-Dame falls into the Seine
events.text: The timber bridge of 1413, carrying some sixty houses, had been neglected by the city. On the morning of 25 October its piles gave way and the whole bridge, houses and all, collapsed into the river. Warned by carpenters, most people had fled. The provost and échevins were jailed for negligence, and the city rebuilt the bridge in stone.

events.title: The St Bartholomew's Day massacre
events.text: Six days after the Protestant Henri of Navarre married the king's sister, the royal council decided to strike the Huguenot leaders gathered for the wedding. At dawn Admiral Coligny was killed near the Louvre and his body thrown from a window; Protestant gentlemen were cut down in the Louvre's court. Parisian militias spread the killing through the city for days; perhaps 2,000 to 3,000 died in Paris.

events.title: Henri IV assassinated
events.text: The king's coach, on its way to the Arsenal, was stopped in the narrow rue de la Ferronnerie, beside the wall of the Innocents, by a cart of hay and a cart of wine. François Ravaillac, a Catholic zealot, climbed on the wheel and stabbed him twice. The king died within minutes. Ravaillac was torn apart by horses on the Place de Grève.

events.title: The storming of the Bastille
events.text: Looking for gunpowder after taking muskets at the Invalides, a crowd of artisans of the faubourg Saint-Antoine, guards and townsmen besieged the fortress. After hours of firing and the arrival of mutinous gardes françaises with cannon, the governor de Launay surrendered at about five. Some 98 attackers died. De Launay was killed on the way to the Hôtel de Ville; seven prisoners were freed.

events.title: The Cemetery of the Innocents is closed
events.text: After a cellar wall in the rue de la Lingerie gave way under the weight of a mass grave, the cemetery was closed in 1780. From 1785 the bones of perhaps two million dead were dug up and carried by night, in black-draped carts followed by priests chanting, to the old quarries south of the city: the Catacombs.

stories.title: A student's year in Gothic Paris
stories.summary: Follow a young clerk from Normandy through a year at the University of Paris in the reign of Saint Louis, from the straw of the lecture room to the steam of the bathhouse.

steps.title: Changing money on the Grand Pont
steps.text: You arrive with a purse of coins of Rouen and Tours from your father. On the Grand Pont the changers weigh them and give you deniers parisis, less their cut; the goldsmith next door shows a silver cup you could never buy.

steps.title: Straw and Aristotle
steps.text: The Norman nation's master lectures before dawn in the rue du Fouarre. You sit on straw, write on wax and learn to dispute: every question has its yes and no. Fees, candles and books eat your money.

steps.title: The cathedral rising
steps.text: At Christmas you hear the polyphony of Notre-Dame's choir, the new music of Pérotin's school, under vaults higher than anything at home. Masons are still at work on the transept; the chancellor here will one day grant your licence.

steps.title: The king's glass house
steps.text: The king shows the Crown of Thorns from his new chapel in the palace. Through the open door you glimpse the upper chapel: walls of glass, red and blue, burning like a jewel box.

steps.title: Market day at the Halles
steps.text: You buy cheap cloth at the Halles and watch a cheating baker turned on the pillory. A Paris crowd is quick to laugh and quick to throw things.

steps.title: A bath at last
steps.text: After the examinations, a bath: the crier calls at dawn that the water is hot. Sitting in a wooden tub with your friends, you count what is left of your father's money.

stories.title: Paris rises: 12–14 July 1789
stories.summary: Three days that began with a speech in a café and ended with a fortress taken: walk with the crowd from the Palais-Royal to the Bastille.

steps.title: A speech in the Palais-Royal
steps.text: News comes that the king has dismissed Necker. In the Palais-Royal garden the young lawyer Camille Desmoulins jumps on a table outside the Café de Foy, pistol in hand: 'To arms!' People pin green leaves to their hats as cockades.

steps.title: Cavalry in the Tuileries
steps.text: Crowds carrying busts of Necker meet the Prince de Lambesc's German cavalry by the Place Louis XV; the horsemen ride into the Tuileries gardens and strike at the crowd. Rumours of a massacre run through the city.

steps.title: The city arms itself
steps.text: At the Hôtel de Ville the electors of Paris form a permanent committee and a citizens' militia, soon the National Guard. Bells ring the alarm; the customs posts burn; everyone wants guns and powder.

steps.title: The fortress falls
steps.text: With muskets from the Invalides but no powder, the crowd turns on the Bastille. Shots from the towers, chains cut on the drawbridge, then the gardes françaises bring cannon. About five o'clock de Launay surrenders.

steps.title: Heads on pikes
steps.text: De Launay is dragged toward the Hôtel de Ville and killed on the Place de Grève; his head is cut off and carried on a pike, with that of the provost Flesselles. The demolition of the Bastille begins the next morning.
